strengths: The core idea of disentangling structural abstraction from semantic content grounding during multimodal table alignment is intuitive, well-motivated, and clearly explained; the design of complementary structure/global-content/local-content alignment objectives is coherent and grounded in the observation that textual serialization formats entangle layout and semantics.

Extensive empirical evaluation spans 21 table understanding and reasoning tasks/benchmarks across four different LVLM backbones (Gemma3, Gemma3n, LLaVA, Qwen3-VL at multiple scales), which provides reasonably broad evidence for the generality of the proposed alignment strategy.

Data efficiency claims are directly tested via a controlled comparison (Textual-10K vs Textual-97K vs DISCO-10K), showing that DISCO with only 10K images is often competitive with or better than models aligned on ~10x more data, supporting the paper's central efficiency claim.

Thorough ablations isolate the contribution of structure alignment vs. local content alignment (Table 1) and of the GSE/SSE stages in Table-GLS (Table 2), helping to substantiate which design choices matter.

The evaluation on non-tabular general benchmarks (ScienceQA, CRPE, HallusionBench, TextVQA) is a valuable check for catastrophic forgetting/over-specialization, and the result that DISCO improves (rather than degrades) general performance while textual alignment can hurt it is a meaningful finding.

Additional analyses (token-efficiency comparison, understanding-reasoning correlation, table-layout/complexity breakdown, and a qualitative case study) add useful interpretive depth beyond the main tables.
weaknesses: The claim that 'DISCO consistently enhances table understanding across all evaluated LVLMs and tasks' is contradicted by the paper's own Table 1/Table 11 results: e.g., for Qwen3-VL-4B, DISCO underperforms both the Textual baseline and even the unaligned model on TSD-Row (21.70 vs 36.60/28.70) and TCE (68.46 vs 81.46), and these regressions are not discussed or explained in the text.

In Table 3, the proposed framework substantially trails the optimized baseline HIPPO on several in-domain and OOD benchmarks (e.g., HiTab: 27.35 vs 63.00; TabFact: 75.41 vs 82.27), which is understated by the framing of 'comparable performance with minimal supervision'; a more balanced discussion of where the gap remains large is needed.

The manuscript reports single-run results throughout with no variance/error bars or multiple seeds, making it hard to judge whether reported gains (some of which are small, e.g., a few points) are statistically meaningful versus noise, especially given the inconsistencies noted above.

The three-stage Table-GLS reasoning process increases token generation substantially (Table 10: ~2x the tokens of CoT), which somewhat undercuts the 'lightweight'/efficiency framing relative to direct answering or CoT, and this trade-off is only briefly acknowledged in the limitations rather than analyzed quantitatively against latency/cost baselines.

The manual assignment of table 'complexity' labels (high/medium/low) in Appendix F is subjective and not validated against any quantitative criterion beyond average rows/columns, weakening the rigor of the layout-robustness analysis in §5.3.

The correlation analysis in §5.4/Figure 4 is qualitative (visual trend across a handful of benchmark points) without a reported correlation coefficient or statistical test, limiting the strength of the claimed relationship between understanding and reasoning performance.

Presentation has multiple typos and inconsistencies (e.g., 'dection' for detection, 'contruction' for construction, inconsistent capitalization of DISCO/DiSCo, an empty code-availability footnote), which detract from polish and reproducibility confidence.

The paper does not report wall-clock or GPU-hour training cost comparisons against the SFT/RL baselines it contrasts itself with, despite efficiency being a central selling point of the work; only the number of training images/samples is compared.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: reducing annotation, training, and tool dependency for LVLM-based table reasoning.
The core idea of disentangling structural layout supervision from semantic content supervision during multimodal alignment is intuitive and reasonably novel in the LVLM-table setting.
Broad empirical scope: experiments span four LVLM backbones (Gemma3, Gemma3n, LLaVA, Qwen3-VL) and 21 understanding/reasoning benchmarks, including in-domain and out-of-domain splits.

Multiple ablations are provided (structure vs. local content alignment; GSE vs. SSE stages; DISCO+CoT vs. Table-GLS), plus supplementary analyses (table-layout robustness, token efficiency, non-tabular transfer, understanding-reasoning correlation), showing non-trivial experimental effort.
The method is training-free at inference (Table-GLS) and uses a small 10K alignment set, which if the claims hold would be a meaningful efficiency contribution.
weaknesses: Central claim that 'DISCO consistently enhances table understanding across all evaluated LVLMs and tasks' is not supported by the data: several entries in Table 1/Table 11 show DISCO underperforming the Textual baseline or even the untrained model on specific metrics (e.g., Qwen3-VL-8B TSD-Column: Textual 79.60 vs DISCO 75.90; Qwen3-VL-4B TSD-Row drops sharply from Textual 36.60 to DISCO 21.70; Gemma3n-E4B TCL-Column drops from None 32.44 to DISCO 31.58). These inconsistencies are not discussed or explained, undermining the 'consistent' framing.

On table reasoning (Table 3), the paper claims the method achieves 'comparable performance' to heavily optimized baselines, but HIPPO substantially outperforms the proposed Qwen3-VL-8B-DISCO+Table-GLS on several benchmarks (e.g., HiTab: 63.00 vs 27.35, more than 2x gap; TabFact: 82.27 vs 75.41), which is a large and unaddressed discrepancy rather than 'comparable' performance.

The ablation in Table 2 shows that removing the Self-refined Sub-table Extraction (SSE) stage actually improves HiTab performance over the full method (31.41 vs 27.35), suggesting the added self-refinement mechanism can hurt performance in some settings; this instability is noted only in passing ('likely due to complex nested structures') without deeper investigation or mitigation.

No variance/statistical significance reporting (single-run numbers throughout); given that many reported improvements are only a few points, the lack of repeated runs or confidence intervals makes it hard to assess whether gains are meaningful or noise.

Baseline comparisons for table reasoning mix different base models, training data sizes, and modalities (e.g., HIPPO on MiniCPM-V with 55.2K samples, Table-R1 with GRPO on Qwen2-VL with 20.6K samples), confounding the attribution of performance differences to the proposed method versus underlying base-model capability.

Table-GLS's multi-stage prompting substantially increases inference token cost (avg ~440-490 tokens vs ~190-240 for CoT, per Appendix G), which is in tension with the paper's core framing of 'efficient' and 'lightweight' reasoning; this trade-off is acknowledged only briefly as a limitation.

The code/data availability footnote is left as an empty placeholder ('Our data and code are available at'), reducing confidence in reproducibility despite claims of an efficient, accessible framework.

Evaluation is confined to the MMTab benchmark suite and its derivative splits; there is no evaluation on independent, more naturalistic or noisy real-world table image datasets, limiting confidence that gains generalize beyond this curated benchmark ecosystem.

The 'self-refinement' in Table-GLS is a single evaluate-then-revise step rather than an iterative refinement loop, and no analysis is given of the intermediate localization quality (precision/recall of predicted row/column indices in Global Structure Exploration), making it hard to diagnose why or when the method succeeds or fails beyond end-task accuracy.
Minor presentation issues (e.g., typos such as 'table size dection', 'primarily focuse') suggest incomplete proofreading.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practical problem: adapting LVLMs to table reasoning with minimal annotation and without external tools, in contrast to costly SFT/RL or tool-augmented pipelines.

The two-stage framework is conceptually clean: DISCO explicitly disentangles structure-only supervision (anonymized layout tokens) from content supervision (global/local descriptions), and Table-GLS operationalizes a global-to-local, plan-then-verify reasoning procedure at inference time without fine-tuning.

Broad empirical coverage: experiments span 21 understanding/reasoning tasks/benchmarks and multiple backbones (Gemma3, Gemma3n, LLaVA-v1.6, Qwen3-VL at several scales), with consistent qualitative trends supporting the core claims.

Good supporting analyses beyond the main tables: ablations isolating structure vs. local content alignment and GSE vs. SSE stages, an understanding-reasoning correlation study, layout/complexity-stratified analysis (Fig. 3/6), token-efficiency accounting (Table 10), and evaluation on non-tabular general benchmarks to check for catastrophic forgetting/over-specialization.

Notable data efficiency: DISCO with only 10K images is often comparable to or better than training with the full 97K/150K MMTab alignment corpus, which is a meaningful practical contribution if it holds up.

The case study (Fig. 5, App. A) is a helpful qualitative illustration of how disentangled alignment plus structured evidence extraction fixes a concrete grounding error made by vanilla CoT and by Table-GLS without DISCO.
weaknesses: Results are not uniformly positive, which undercuts some of the stated conclusions: e.g., in Table 3, Gemma3n-E4B-DISCO Table-GLS underperforms plain DA on several columns (AIT-QA 59.10 vs 64.77, TabMCQ 32.17 vs 33.24, InfoTabs 58.76 vs 52.74 is a gain but HiTab is mixed), and in Table 1 DISCO sometimes underperforms the Textual(10K) baseline for the same backbone (e.g., Qwen3-VL-4B OOD/TSD-Row: 21.70 vs 36.60; TSD-Row 21.70 vs 36.60). The paper's narrative ('DISCO consistently enhances...', 'Table-GLS outperforms DA on almost all benchmarks') is stated more strongly than the tables support in places.

No statistical significance testing or repeated runs are reported; several evaluation sets are quite small (e.g., TabMCQ has only 50 tables/1029 samples, AIT-QA 111 tables), so single-run percentage-point differences of a few points may not be robust, yet they are used to support fine-grained claims (e.g., about specific task categories benefiting most).

Baseline comparisons in Table 3 mix different backbones, training data scales, and paradigms (Table-LLaVA, Qwen2-VL-7B-Table-R1, MiniCPM-V-2.6-HIPPO vs. the paper's own Gemma3n/Qwen3-VL models), making the 'comparable to optimized LVLMs' claim only loosely apples-to-apples since backbone capability differences are conflated with method differences.

Table-GLS's efficiency claims are undercut by its own token-cost analysis: DISCO+Table-GLS uses roughly 2x the tokens of vanilla CoT (Table 10), and the paper's own limitations section acknowledges this — the 'lightweight' framing in the abstract/intro is thus somewhat optimistic relative to the actual inference cost multiplier from three sequential LLM calls.

Reproducibility is weakened by an incomplete data/code release: the footnote 'Our data and code are available at' has no actual URL/link, and several implementation choices (e.g., exact anonymization rules for merged/hierarchical headers, full prompt variants beyond the ones listed) are only partially specified.

The manuscript contains several typographical/grammatical errors (e.g., 'table size dection', 'Merged Cell Dection', 'existing method', 'focuse', 'Contruction' in the appendix header) and imprecise notation (e.g., undefined table-position variables m, n reused inconsistently across understanding and content-alignment sections) that reduce polish and occasionally clarity.

The 'Impact Statements' section is essentially a boilerplate non-statement ('none of which we feel must be specifically highlighted'), which is a missed opportunity given the paper concerns automated reasoning over potentially sensitive tabular domains (financial, medical, government data) mentioned in the introduction.

Some interpretive claims are stated with more confidence than the evidence directly supports, e.g., that DISCO 'internalizes the universal logic of tabular organization' — this is inferred from OOD margins on a handful of benchmarks rather than directly probed or validated by a targeted diagnostic.

strengths: Addresses a practical and important problem: adapting LVLMs for table reasoning without costly SFT/RL fine-tuning or external tool dependencies, which is a meaningful efficiency contribution.

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning 21 table understanding/reasoning tasks, multiple LVLM backbones (Gemma3, Gemma3n, LLaVA, Qwen3-VL at 4B/8B/32B scales), and both open- and closed-source models, lending reasonable breadth to the claims.

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contributions of structure vs. content alignment (w/o TL), and of the GSE/SSE/EGR stages in Table-GLS, as well as a revision-mechanism analysis with a small human evaluation.

Demonstrates that DISCO does not degrade (and often improves) performance on non-tabular general benchmarks (ScienceQA, CRPE, HallusionBench, TextVQA), addressing catastrophic forgetting concerns directly.

Useful practical analyses beyond accuracy: inference latency/token-count comparisons against tool-augmented (REFOCUS) and preference-optimized (HIPPO) baselines, and prompt-sensitivity checks for Table-GLS, which strengthen claims of robustness and efficiency.

Data efficiency claim is reasonably supported: DISCO with only 10K images is shown to match or exceed textual alignment trained on 97K images across several settings, and a data-scale ablation (5K-20K) supports stability.
weaknesses: Potential train/test overlap is not clearly ruled out: the DISCO alignment corpus (Table 9) is drawn from the same benchmark families used for downstream evaluation (WTQ, HiTab, TabFact, InfoTabs, TAT-QA, etc., Tables 3/11); the paper does not explicitly confirm disjoint table images/splits between alignment and evaluation, which is important for the validity of the reported gains.

Novelty is somewhat incremental: the structure/content disentanglement is essentially content-masking of serialized table formats plus global/local captioning objectives, and Table-GLS's plan→extract→answer pattern closely resembles existing structured/self-refine CoT strategies (e.g., RoT, REFOCUS-style evidence grounding) adapted to tables rather than a fundamentally new reasoning paradigm.

Result trends are not fully consistent: DISCO sometimes underperforms the Textual baseline on individual sub-tasks (e.g., TSD-Column for Qwen3-VL-8B: 75.90 vs. 79.60 for Textual), and these mixed results are not discussed in depth, weakening confidence in the claimed general superiority.

No variance/seed information or statistical significance testing is reported for the many head-to-head comparisons, several of which involve small margins, making it hard to assess robustness of the conclusions, especially in a zero-shot evaluation setting.

Coverage of the full reasoning pipeline is incomplete for larger/closed-source models: Table 4 evaluates Qwen3-VL-32B and GPT-5.4-mini on only 4 of the 8 reasoning benchmarks used for the main results, limiting the strength of scaling claims.

Table-GLS roughly doubles token generation relative to vanilla CoT (Table 15), and although the paper frames this as a favorable trade-off, the added latency (Table 8, ~15-20x that of HIPPO) may be prohibitive for latency-sensitive applications despite being 'tool-free'.

Manuscript has noticeable presentation issues (e.g., repeated typo 'dection' for 'detection', a broken figure reference 'As shown in Figure,' in Sec 3.2, grammatical inconsistencies) that suggest incomplete proofreading and slightly undermine confidence in careful preparation of the submission.

The human evaluation of the self-refinement mechanism's reliability (Section 5.7) is based on only 50 samples judged by 4 undergraduates with no inter-annotator agreement reported, which is a fairly weak basis for the reliability claim.

strengths: The core idea of disentangling table structure abstraction from semantic content grounding during multimodal alignment is a reasonable and interpretable motivation, addressing a genuine limitation of prior HTML/Markdown/LaTeX-based alignment approaches.

The proposed Table-GLS inference pipeline (global structure exploration, self-refined sub-table extraction, evidence-grounded reasoning) is training-free and tool-free, which is practically appealing compared to methods requiring OCR/symbolic executors or costly RL fine-tuning.

The experimental scope is broad, covering 21 tasks/benchmarks, multiple backbone LVLMs of different scales (4B-32B), and several ablations (component removal, prompt sensitivity, revision mechanism, token efficiency, non-tabular generalization).
Data efficiency claims (10K vs 97K/150K samples) are a potentially useful practical contribution if validated more rigorously.
The paper includes some thoughtful auxiliary analyses, such as understanding-reasoning correlation and impact of table layout complexity.
weaknesses: Many reported gains are inconsistent or even negative: e.g., for Qwen3-VL-4B, TSD Row drops sharply from Textual (36.60) to DISCO (21.70), and in Table 14 the effect of alignment data scale (5K/10K/15K/20K) is highly non-monotonic without any variance/error bars, undermining claims of robust, consistent improvement and data efficiency.

The self-refinement mechanism, a central claimed innovation, is only validated through an informal human study with 4 undergraduate annotators on just 50 samples—this is far too small and subjective a sample to substantiate reliability claims about the LVLM's self-correction ability.

No statistical significance testing or repeated runs are reported anywhere in the paper, despite substantial score fluctuations across settings (e.g., ablation of the Hal-Check and SSE steps producing counter-intuitive, unexplained results such as removing SSE improving HiTab performance), making it hard to trust that reported differences reflect real effects rather than noise.

The closed-source baseline 'GPT-5.4-mini' referenced in Tables 3/4 does not correspond to any known publicly documented model, raising concerns about experimental validity, reproducibility, or possible errors/fabrication in this comparison.

The paper selectively highlights favorable comparisons (e.g., against Table-R1/HIPPO on OOD sets) while results such as HiTab (27.35 for DISCO+Table-GLS vs. 63.00 for HIPPO) show the proposed lightweight approach substantially underperforming heavily optimized baselines, yet this large gap is not discussed or analyzed in the main text.

Table-GLS's claimed 'efficiency' is undercut by its own token-usage analysis (Table 15), which shows roughly 2x the token consumption of vanilla CoT, and inference-time results (Table 8) show it is much slower than HIPPO while only moderately faster than REFOCUS with lower accuracy on some datasets—the efficiency narrative is therefore only partially supported.

The multi-stage prompting pipeline (three sequential LVLM calls per query) is conceptually similar in spirit to a tool/agentic pipeline despite being framed as 'no external tools'; this framing may overstate the novelty/simplicity relative to prior agentic or tool-augmented approaches.

Presentation has multiple typos and unclear phrasing (e.g., 'dection', 'strucuture', 'Contruction', ambiguous figure references such as 'As shown in Figure' without a number), which detracts from the professionalism and clarity of the manuscript.

The comparison baselines for table understanding (TableLlama+Oracle/OCR near-zero performance, older Table-LLaVA) are weak and outdated, making the reported improvements look artificially large without stronger, more recent LVLM-based table baselines for context.

strengths: The core idea of disentangling structure and content during multimodal alignment (via anonymized-structure prediction plus global/local content grounding) is intuitive, well-motivated, and clearly distinct from prior approaches that align tables with entangled linearized text (HTML/Markdown/LaTeX).

Strong data efficiency: DISCO with only 10K images is shown to match or exceed alignment with the full 97K/150K MMTab corpus across most understanding tasks and multiple backbone LVLMs (Gemma3, Gemma3n, LLaVA, Qwen3-VL of varying scale), and the paper includes a data-scale sweep (5K-20K) supporting this claim.

The Table-GLS reasoning framework is training-free and tool-free, and the paper provides a reasonably thorough set of ablations (GSE/SSE removal, comparison to CoT/RoT, prompt-sensitivity checks, revision-mechanism human evaluation) that support the design choices.

Broad evaluation scope: 21 tasks/benchmarks spanning table understanding (TSD/TCL/RCE/MCD/TCE and their OOD variants) and table reasoning (QA and fact verification, in-domain and OOD), plus evaluation on non-tabular general benchmarks to check for catastrophic forgetting/negative transfer.

Useful auxiliary analyses beyond headline numbers: understanding-reasoning correlation study, inference-cost/latency comparison against a tool-augmented baseline (REFOCUS) and a preference-optimized baseline (HIPPO), and token-efficiency analysis, which help contextualize the practical trade-offs of the method.
weaknesses: Results are not uniformly consistent with the paper's strong claims of "consistent" improvement: e.g., DISCO underperforms the Textual baseline on several individual metrics (Qwen3-VL-8B OOD-TSD column 44.40 vs Textual's 50.40, TSD-column 75.90 vs 79.60, TCL Row lower than Textual for several models in Table 14), and Table-GLS actually hurts performance relative to direct answering on HiTab (27.35 vs 33.50/35.47), which is only partially explained post hoc via the SSE ablation.

Comparisons to optimized baselines (Table-R1, HIPPO, Table-LLaVA) are confounded by different backbone models (Qwen2-VL, MiniCPM-V, LLaVA) and different training data scales, making it difficult to attribute performance differences cleanly to the proposed alignment/reasoning strategy versus base-model capability differences.

The "efficient"/"lightweight" framing for Table-GLS is somewhat at odds with the reported inference cost: it roughly doubles token generation versus CoT (Table 15) and requires noticeably higher per-sample latency than HIPPO (Table 8), so efficiency gains are primarily relative to tool-augmented methods (REFOCUS) rather than an absolute reduction versus simple baselines.

The reliability assessment of the self-refinement mechanism relies on only 50 sampled instances judged by 4 undergraduates, which is a small and informal evaluation for a claim central to justifying the SSE stage's design.

Definition of "unseen"/OOD table structures is somewhat loose — OOD sets are simply different benchmarks (AIT-QA, PubHealthTab, TabMCQ, LoTNLG) rather than tables constructed to rigorously test structural generalization, so claims of superior generalization to "unseen table structures" are only indirectly supported.

No statistical significance testing or repeated-run variance is reported anywhere in the paper; single-run point estimates are used throughout for all comparisons, including fairly small performance gaps (e.g., a few points on some tasks) presented as clear wins.

Presentation issues: several typos/inconsistent terminology throughout (e.g., "dection", "contruction", "optimizated", "incorprate"), and the code/data repository link is left blank, so reproducibility currently depends entirely on a promised future release rather than verifiable artifacts at review time.

Some ablation ndings (e.g., "+ Hal Check" not improving performance, SSE removal improving HiTab) are reported but not deeply analyzed or explained beyond speculation, leaving open questions about robustness of the specific design choices to different table types.
